analysis.one_liner: Weakens debt-collection rules and exempts first-lien mortgage servicers from key consumer protections.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the House Banking Committee and its consumer credit subcommittee in November 1999 and never received a hearing or vote; it died when that Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have loosened the Fair Debt Collection Practices Act, the law that sets rules for how debt collectors may treat people. It would have let collection activity continue during the 30-day window when consumers are supposed to be able to dispute a debt, cap the attorney fees a collector might have to pay, and shield collectors from liability when they claim they were following court rules. It would also have exempted servicers of first-lien mortgages from major debt-collection rules, replacing them with a lighter notice requirement. The bill was introduced by Rep. Jack Metcalf with one cosponsor and never advanced past a subcommittee referral.
analysis.who_benefits: Debt collection companies and mortgage servicers. Collection firms would face fewer lawsuits and lower exposure to class-action damages and attorney fees, and would be able to keep contacting and pursuing consumers during the dispute window unless the consumer actively asked them to stop. Mortgage servicers would be freed from the Fair Debt Collection Practices Act's bans on false or misleading statements and its full validation requirements when collecting delinquent first-lien mortgages.

how_it_helps.text: It redefines 'communication' under the debt collection law to exclude court filings and nonjudicial foreclosure steps, so those actions could not themselves count as violations.

It allows collection activity and communications to continue during the 30-day initial notice period unless the consumer requests a stop, shifting the burden onto the consumer rather than waiting for the dispute period to end.

It adds a safe harbor: a debt collector cannot be held liable for a violation that resulted from good-faith compliance with federal or state rules of civil procedure or a nonjudicial foreclosure proceeding.

It caps the attorney fees a consumer's lawyer can recover when enforcing the law at no more than the amount awarded in the case, and adds the size of actual damages as a factor courts must weigh when setting awards.

It exempts servicers of first-lien mortgage loans from the law's prohibitions on false or misleading representations and its validation-of-debt requirements, substituting a notice at least 30 days before acceleration of the debt and a validation statement available on written request — while explicitly not requiring the servicer to delay foreclosure while the request is pending.

analysis.who_pays: Consumers who owe debts, especially homeowners facing foreclosure. People disputing a debt would have to affirmatively request a stop to collection activity during the validation window, and collectors would gain a shield from liability whenever they claim good-faith reliance on court procedures. Homeowners would lose the debt-collection law's protection against false or misleading statements and its full validation rights from their mortgage servicer, with no requirement that the servicer pause a foreclosure while verifying the debt. The attorney-fee cap would make it harder for consumers' lawyers to take small-value cases.
analysis.who_pays_short: Consumers in debt, especially homeowners facing foreclosure

drawbacks.text: The bill reverses the default in the dispute window: under current law, collection generally pauses for 30 days so the consumer can verify the debt; the bill would let collection continue unless the consumer asks it to stop, putting the burden on the person being pursued.

Exempting first-lien mortgage servicers from the ban on false or misleading representations and from full debt-validation duties removes a check on servicer conduct at exactly the stage — delinquency and foreclosure — where errors and misstatements do the most damage, and the bill expressly says a servicer need not delay foreclosure because a consumer requested a validation statement.

Capping attorney fees at the amount awarded would reduce lawyers' willingness to take small consumer claims, since these cases often turn on fees; many violations involve modest amounts, so the cap could leave violations without a practical remedy.

The safe harbor for 'good faith compliance' with rules of civil procedure and nonjudicial foreclosure would give collectors a broad new defense, since much collection activity runs through the courts.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits flow to collectors and servicers in the form of reduced litigation exposure and simpler collection procedures; the stated rationale is lower credit costs. The costs fall on consumers, who would lose the quiet 30-day dispute window, give up protection against misleading statements from mortgage servicers, and face a broad good-faith defense for collectors. For anyone disputing a debt or fighting a foreclosure, the trade is clearly worse; the promised savings in credit costs are indirect and speculative.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Banking Committee and then to its consumer credit subcommittee, where it sat without a hearing or vote until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Jack Metcalf introduced the bill on November 17, 1999, with one cosponsor, Rep. Virgil Goode.
The House referred it to the Committee on Banking and Financial Services the same day.
On December 2, 1999, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Financial Institutions and Consumer Credit, and no further action was taken.
No hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote ever occurred, and the bill expired when the 106th Congress ended in January 2001.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Consumers, who kept the existing debt-collection protections — the 30-day dispute window, full validation rights, and the ban on misleading statements by mortgage servicers — that the bill would have trimmed. Debt collectors and servicers avoided a partial loosening of the law but lost nothing they already had.

for.name: Rep. Jack Metcalf
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to amend the Fair Debt Collection Practices Act and referred to its title of reducing the cost of credit.

for.name: Rep. Virgil Goode
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction, the only cosponsor it attracted.

against.name: House Committee on Banking and Financial Services
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and took no further action — no hearing or markup was scheduled.

against.name: Rep. Marge Roukema
against.role: Chair, Subcommittee on Financial Institutions and Consumer Credit
against.what_they_did: The subcommittee to which the bill was referred never acted on it; it sat there until the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: Only two members supported the bill — one Republican sponsor and one Democratic cosponsor — and no vote or recorded opposition ever occurred, so no partisan pattern can be measured.

industries.note: The bill narrows what counts as a prohibited communication, lets collection continue through the dispute window by default, adds a good-faith safe harbor tied to court procedure, and limits attorney fees and weighs damages downward — all reducing collectors' legal exposure. The cost falls on consumers disputing debts.

First-lien servicers would be exempt from the ban on false or misleading representations and from full debt-validation duties, with a lighter notice-and-request system and no requirement to delay foreclosure while a validation request is pending. This removes a consumer check precisely during delinquency and foreclosure.

The attorney-fee cap (fees cannot exceed the award) and the expanded treatment of related class actions reduce the economics of small consumer cases and aggregate private enforcement, leaving violations less likely to be litigated.
